tagline: The heaviest soaring bird, which almost never needs to flap
summary: A huge black-and-white vulture of the Andes, with a white neck ruff and wings spanning about 3.2 m. Flight recorders fitted to wild condors in Patagonia showed they flap for only 1% of their time in the air, riding thermals and mountain winds instead. One bird flew for more than five hours without a single wingbeat.

stats.size: 97.5–128 cm long with a wingspan of about 3.2 m; 7.7–15 kg, males larger than females
stats.habitat: Open mountains, high canyons, cliffs, steppe and desert, where carrion can be spotted from the air
stats.range: The Andes and Pacific side of South America, from Colombia and north-western Venezuela to Tierra del Fuego

facts.title: One wingbeat in a hundred
facts.text: Custom 'flight recorders' that logged every wingbeat across more than 216 hours of flight showed that young wild condors in Patagonia flapped for only 1% of their flight time. More than 75% of that flapping came during take-off.

facts.title: 172 km on still wings
facts.text: One tagged condor flew for more than five hours without flapping, covering about 172 km. Even in winter, when thermals are weak, the researchers predict condors need to flap for only about two seconds per kilometre.

facts.title: Wings of a glider
facts.text: At around 3.2 m, the Andean condor's wingspan is the longest of any land bird. Gaps between its spread primary feathers help it soar, and it rides the thermals rising off cliff faces for hours with very little effort.

facts.title: Searching by sight
facts.text: Andean condors find carrion by sight, scanning the ground from thousands of feet up. They mostly scavenge, but sometimes take small animals such as marmots and rabbits.

facts.title: Comb and eye colour
facts.text: Males are larger than females and have a fleshy comb on the head, which females lack. Males have yellow eyes, while females' eyes are red.

facts.title: A slow start in life
facts.text: Andean condors breed only every two to three years, laying a single egg on a bare cliff ledge, and both parents share the 54–58 days of incubation. For a bird that breeds so slowly, lead from ammunition and persecution by farmers are serious threats.

notes: Flight figures (1% flapping, >216 h, >75% at take-off, >5 h and ~172 km without flapping, ~2 s per km in winter) are verbatim from the Williams et al. 2020 abstract and significance statement, read in full text via Europe PMC (PMC7395523). The tagged birds were immatures (eight condors) from Bariloche, Argentina, 2013–2018. Williams et al. call it the 'world's heaviest soaring bird'. The wingspan, mass, elevation (up to 5,500 m), diet, incubation and 'breed every 2 to 3 years' are from Animal Diversity Web. ADW still lists the species as Near Threatened, which is outdated; status is taken from IUCN (VU, 2020, confirmed via GBIF's IUCN checklist and the DOI handle). The range, comb, eye colour, 'one chick every other year' and 'shot and poisoned' are from the Peregrine Fund; ADW also lists lead ammunition and persecution by farmers. Order: Cathartiformes is used, as in most current bird checklists; the GBIF backbone places Cathartidae in Accipitriformes. Regions: andes-patagonia only (the Venezuelan and Colombian Andes are not a separate region). Categories: fliers only. It is a scavenger, not an apex predator, and VU does not meet the EN/CR bar for 'endangered'. Image alt-1: the Commons file name says 'male in flight Torres del Paine', but its description reads 'immature in flight, Farellones, Andes Mountains, Chile' (apparently copied from a sister upload). The caption therefore says only 'Chilean Andes' and does not give an age or sex. Only one gallery image is used; the others found were zoo birds or near-duplicates. iucnredlist.org and gbif.org web pages return 403 to scripted requests, so they were checked through the DOI handle API and the GBIF API.
